newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada judge frees accused in stowaways case.
newsitem.headline: Canada judge frees accused in stowaways case.

text.p: A Canadian judge on Thursday freed six Taiwanese sailors accused of killing three Romanian stowaways at sea, saying he had no jurisdiction to extradite the men to Romania to face murder charges.

Nova Scotia Supreme Court Judge Michael MacDonald said that if he had jurisdiction in the case, he would have put the men, all officers of the merchant ship Maersk Dubai, on trial on manslaughter and second-degree murder charges for casting the stowaways adrift, which resulted in their presumed deaths.
MacDonald said the officers were free to go from the court. But they did not have travel documents needed to leave Canada immediately as their passports were seized last May.

Filipino sailors, who fled the Maersk Dubai in this port city on Canada's Atlantic coast last May, accused the ship's captain and officers of forcing the stowaways overboard in two separate incidents. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police stormed the ship and arrested its captain and officers.

Defence lawyers acknowledged that two stowaways were forced off the ship in March 1996, but said they were given lifejackets, food and water and were in sight of land when cast overboard. The Filipino sailors said another Romanian stowaway was thrown off the ship in May.
The bodies of the missing stowaways, Radu Danciu, 29, Petre Sangeorzan, 20, and Gheorghe Mihoc, 18, have not been found, and Romanian investigators said their families have not heard from them.

"Prosecutors in Taiwan will probably be filing charges against the officers when they return," said Andrew Hsia, deputy representative for the Taipei economic and cultural office based in Ottawa. "I know they will return to Taiwan."
Canadian Justice Minister Allan Rock said in a statement that the Canadian government prosecution, acting on behalf of Romania, had appealed the decision.

He said a single judge from the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal had rejected a prosecution request at a hearing on Thursday afternoon to stay the effects of the Thursday morning decision -- effectively to keep the officers under arrest for now.
The minister added that on Friday morning the prosecution would lodge an appeal before the full Court of Appeal of the refusal to stay the effects of MacDonald's decision.

Rock noted that Judge MacDonald had concluded that there was sufficient evidence to commit the officers for criminal acts and had only discharged them on the grounds that he did not have the jurisdiction to extradite them to Romania.
Defence lawyers complained that the officers should be allowed to leave Canada, but without passports, they appeared unable to leave the country until the appeal was heard.
Taiwan officials told Reuters they promised Ottawa that the officers would not be issued new passports, but said Taipei was "considering other initiatives."

In his decision, MacDonald said he did not have the authority to commit the men to trial in Canada because the alleged crimes occurred on a Taiwanese ship in international waters, rather than on a Romanian ship or territory.
The judge added, however, that there was enough evidence presented during a 41-day hearing to warrant issuing manslaughter and second-degree murder charges against the ship's captain and officers.

In what has become an international diplomatic dispute, Bucharest wants the officers extradited to Romania, while Taiwan says it has jurisdiction because the ship was operating in international waters under the Taiwanese flag.
China, claiming sovereignty over Taiwan, insists Beijing should decide the officers' fate.
